Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e111.summary: Rubric giving the title of Prologue Question 2: on what a science derives from its subject.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e118.summary: Divisio paragraph: having treated the subject of theology in itself, Giles turns to the five features a science derives from its subject (order, dignity, unity, distinction, necessity, as listed in Q.1), reduces them to four by folding distinction into unity, and orders the inquiry as order, dignity, unity, necessity; since order among sciences is a matter of subalternation, the question of order is split into three articles — whether theology is subalternated to a human science, to some other science, and whether it subalternates human sciences to itself.
claims: Unity and distinction of a science come to the same thing, since what makes a thing one also makes it distinct from others.
The order of one science to another consists in subalternation.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e180.summary: Rubric giving the title of Article 1: whether theology is subalternated to any human science.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e189.summary: Opening arguments that theology is subalternated to metaphysics: (1) when subject falls under subject, science falls under science, and God as a distinct being falls under common being, the subject of metaphysics; (2) theology speaks of God in a mode of wonder, which arises from ignorance of causes (Metaph. 1), while metaphysics gives causes without wonder, and a science that gives the cause subalternates one that does not.
claims: Theology's subject, as a distinct being, seems to fall under the common subject of metaphysics.
A science that treats something by giving its cause subalternates one that treats the same thing without its cause, in wonder.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e248.summary: Further opening arguments: (3) theology is subalternated to natural philosophy, since it asserts God's infinite power which Aristotle proves in Physics 8 from motion in infinite time, and the proving science subalternates the narrating one; (4) theology is subalternated to all sciences, since, like perspective drawing propositions from geometry, it takes propositions from all of them. Sed contra: what excels all sciences and is served by all is subalternated to none; theology, being even more principally about God than metaphysics (which Aristotle calls 'divine'), is the most divine science, served by all.
claims: Theology appears to depend on natural philosophy for the proof of God's infinite power.
Theology appears subalternated to all sciences since it borrows propositions from them.
Since theology is more principally about God than metaphysics, it is more properly the divine science and is subalternated to none.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e311.summary: Editorial 'Resolutio' summarizing the article: theology is subalternated to no human science.
claims: Theology is subalternated to no human science.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e319.summary: Opens the determinatio by announcing three modes of subalternation, and names the first: when one science serves (ancillatur) another.
claims: There are three modes of subalternation, the first being when one science serves another.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e330.summary: Explains the first mode of subalternation as service (famulatus): it counts as subalternation because the serving science is ordered by the one it serves; this is the mode by which all sciences serve metaphysics (Metaph. 1), grounded in the principle that the science which considers the best in a genus regulates all others in that genus, so metaphysics, considering the best among beings, regulates all humanly invented sciences and verifies their principles.
claims: Service (famulatus) is a kind of subalternation because the serving science is ordered by the served.
The science that considers the best in a genus regulates the other sciences of that genus.
Metaphysics regulates all humanly invented sciences because it considers the best among beings.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e376.summary: Introduces the second and third modes of subalternation, taken from Posterior Analytics 1, distinguished as non-univocal and quasi-univocal (sentence continues into next paragraph).
claims: The second and third modes of subalternation, from Post. An. 1, differ as non-univocal and quasi-univocal.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e385.summary: Analyzes the non-univocal (second) mode, exemplified by perspective under geometry: the subalternating science gives the propter quid of what the subalternated gives the quia, and four conditions are required — the two are in some way about the same thing; the subalternated adds something to the subalternating science's object (visual line adds to line), because the propter quid science is more abstract; the addition is not caused by the principles of what it is added to (unlike 'curved', which belongs to the same science as 'line'); and the addition is compossible with it (there is no science of 'white line').
claims: In the non-univocal mode, the subalternating science gives the propter quid of what the subalternated science knows quia.
This mode requires four conditions: sameness of object in some way, an addition, an addition not caused by the subject's own principles, and compossibility of the addition.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e500.summary: Ranks the four conditions of non-univocal subalternation: two (compossibility of the addition and its not arising from the subject's principles) are required only per accidens, as conditions sine quibus non (sentence continues).
claims: Compossibility and non-derivation of the addition are only per accidens conditions of subalternation.
concepts: per se vs. per accidens conditions

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e516.summary: Completes the ranking: the first two conditions (sameness of object in some way and addition) are required per se and directly, and from them follows that one science gives the propter quid and the other the quia.
claims: The per se conditions of subalternation are sameness of object and addition, from which the quia/propter quid relation follows.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e530.summary: Describes the third, quasi-univocal mode of subalternation: both sciences treat the same thing, but the higher in a subtle and the lower in a coarse mode, as mathematical harmonics and harmonics by ear, or astronomy and the sailors' practical knowledge of the stars' courses.
claims: In the quasi-univocal mode the subalternating science treats the same object subtly, the subalternated coarsely.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e574.summary: Applies the three modes to show theology is subalternated to no human science. Not to metaphysics: not by the first mode, since theology attains God (the best among beings) more principally than metaphysics, which should rather serve it (to be taken up in Art. 3); not by the second, since what theology says of God is above reason and no rational science can give its propter quid; not by the third, since there the higher science knows more and higher things, whereas theology knows higher things of God, and metaphysics does not treat God as restorer and glorifier. Not to the special sciences: none considers God, the best among beings — not even natural philosophy, the most universal of them (Physics 2) — and the second and third modes require the same substance to be treated by both sciences, which never holds for God and a special human science.
claims: Theology is not subalternated to metaphysics in any of the three modes.
No rational science can give the propter quid of theological truths, which are above reason.
Theology knows higher things about God than metaphysics, reversing the third mode's requirement.
No special human science considers God, so none can subalternate theology.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e743.summary: Replies to the first two arguments: (1) subject falling under subject in the way theology's falls under metaphysics' is insufficient without the specific conditions of the modes of subalternation, which are not met; (2) theology speaks of God in wonder not because metaphysics supplies causes of what it narrates but because its content is higher than metaphysics, being above reason.
claims: Inclusion of one subject under another is not sufficient for subalternation.
Theology's wonder arises from the height of its content, not from ignorance of causes known to metaphysics.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e787.summary: Replies to the remaining arguments: (3) theology presupposes God's infinite power from uncreated wisdom, not from natural philosophy; (4) theology takes propositions from all sciences not as rules governing it (as perspective takes from geometry) but as ordering them to its service, as the military art uses bridle-making, the superior using the inferior; this also better answers (3): even if theology borrows the proof of infinite power from physics, it does so in subordinating, not subordinated, fashion.
claims: Theology derives the truth of God's infinite power from uncreated wisdom.
Theology uses propositions from other sciences in obsequium sui, as a superior art uses an inferior one, not as regulating principles.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e845.summary: Rubric giving the title of Article 2: whether theology is subalternated to any science.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e852.summary: First argument that theology is subalternated to no science at all: it is not subalternated to any human science (Art. 1), and the only other science is divine science, but nothing is subalternated to itself.
claims: Apart from human sciences there is only divine science, which is theology itself.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e872.summary: Second argument: theology joins us to the noblest end, so it is noblest and placed under none. Sed contra: whatever presupposes principles without proving them is subalternated to the science from which it presupposes them; theology presupposes the articles of faith as principles; so it is subalternated to the science from which it receives them.
claims: Theology, as noblest, seems to be under no other science.
A science that presupposes unproven principles is subalternated to the science in which they are known; theology so presupposes the articles of faith.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e892.summary: Editorial 'Resolutio' summarizing the article: theology is not subalternated to any science of wayfarers by any of the three assigned modes (implying it is subalternated to a higher science in a distinct way).
claims: Theology is not subalternated to any science of wayfarers by any of the three modes.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e902.summary: Determinatio: every science proceeds from principles, since science is the habit of conclusions and intellect the habit of principles; as principles differ by knower (known to all vs. to the wise, per Boethius), they can differ by science (known in the science that uses them or in another); a science using principles not self-evident but made clear in another is subalternated to it. Since theology uses the articles of faith, which are not self-evident to us, and yet is a science (Augustine, De Trinitate 13), its principles must be evident in a higher science (sentence continues).
claims: Science is the habit of conclusions, intellect the habit of principles.
A science using principles declared in another science is subalternated to that science.
Since the articles of faith are not self-evident to us yet theology is a science, they must be evident in some higher science.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e986.summary: Completes the argument: the only higher science is God's knowledge or that of the blessed, so theology is subalternated to divine science or to the science of the blessed; but none of the modes found among human sciences fits exactly — not the first, since theology too is principally about the best (God); not the second or third, since in matters concerning God there is properly no quia and propter quid, everything in God being God and uncaused.
claims: Theology is subalternated to God's own knowledge or to the knowledge of the blessed.
None of the three human modes of subalternation applies strictly to this relation.
In God there is no distinction of quia and propter quid, since all that is in God is God and uncaused.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1036.summary: Qualifies the preceding: though this subalternation is not identical with any human mode, it resembles each — the first, because the science of the blessed grasps the same best object more fully; the second, because principles assumed by the theologian are not evident in theology but are evident to the blessed, as geometry's are not evident in perspective; the third, because the theologian sees unity of essence and trinity of persons coarsely what God and the blessed see subtly, as sailors and astronomers regard the stars.
claims: Theology's subalternation to the science of the blessed resembles all three human modes analogically.
Theology's principles are not evident within theology but are evident to the blessed.
The theologian grasps the Trinity coarsely what God and the blessed grasp subtly.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1097.summary: Replies: (1) theology is subalternated not to itself but to divine science, which is twofold, uncreated and created, the created being of wayfarers or of the blessed; (2) 'noblest' is either in its genus or simpliciter: theology is noblest among wayfarers' sciences, but the science of the blessed and God's science are nobler and theology can be subalternated to them.
claims: Divine science is uncreated or created, and created divine science belongs either to wayfarers or to the blessed.
Theology is noblest among the sciences of wayfarers but not noblest simpliciter.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1143.summary: Rubric giving the title of Article 3: whether theology subalternates the human sciences to itself.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1161.summary: Statement of the third question: whether theology subalternates the other human sciences to itself.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1170.summary: Argument for: a science that gives the cause of what other sciences say subalternates them; theology gives knowledge of God, the cause of everything treated in the other sciences; so it subalternates them all.
claims: Because theology gives knowledge of God, the cause of all, it seems to subalternate all sciences.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1186.summary: Second argument for: subalternation means being under another, and every human science is under theology as under a worthier one. Sed contra: a subalternated science receives its principles from the subalternating one, but no science receives its principles from theology.
claims: Every human science is under theology as under a worthier science.
No human science receives its principles from theology.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1205.summary: Editorial 'Resolutio' summarizing the article: in some way the human sciences are subalternated to theology.
claims: The human sciences are in some way subalternated to theology.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1214.summary: Determinatio: of the three modes, the second (receiving principles) and third (treating the same object coarsely, which would require the other sciences to treat God as restorer and glorifier) do not hold between theology and human sciences; only the first mode, attaining the best, applies. Analyzing metaphysics' subalternation of the other sciences, Giles distinguishes two grounds: metaphysics attains the best (God) as far as natural reason allows, so all sciences serve it and it alone is free (Metaph. 1, Ethics 1: end under end, science under science); and it attains the best by reason's mode, so it declares the common principles on which all sciences rest. Theology has the first ground but not the second, since it attains God by revelation, not reason; hence all sciences serve theology and are taken into its service, though it does not declare their principles; and since theology attains the best more than metaphysics, the sciences serve it more, and metaphysics itself, compared to theology, is not free but its handmaid.
claims: Human sciences are subalternated to theology only by the first mode, because theology attains the highest good which they do not.
Metaphysics subalternates other sciences both because it attains the best and because it declares common principles by reason's mode.
Theology attains the best by revelation, not by reason, so it does not declare the principles of other sciences.
Metaphysics, compared to theology, is not free but a handmaid.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1422.summary: Replies: (1) giving the cause of what another science says suffices for subalternation only if it is given by reason's mode and presupposed by the lower science, which is not the case with theology, so the sciences are subalternated to it only by reason of the end; (2) all human sciences are under theology as worthier insofar as it attains the best; (3, sed contra) subalternation by the first mode does not require receiving principles. The paragraph ends in corrupted transcription.
claims: Theology subalternates human sciences only by reason of the end, not by supplying causes or principles.
Subalternation by the first mode does not require that the lower science take its principles from the higher.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1483.summary: Rubric giving the title of Article 4: whether theology is a worthier science than the other human sciences.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1496.summary: Transition: having treated theology's order to other sciences, which it derives from its subject, Giles turns to its dignity, also derived from its subject.
claims: Theology's dignity, like its order, derives from its subject.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1509.summary: First argument against theology's greater dignity: the more a science makes us know, the nobler it is; knowing is through causes (Post. An. 1, Phys. 1); human sciences give causes while theology seems merely to narrate; so they are nobler.
claims: Sciences that give causes produce more knowledge than theology, which narrates.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1530.summary: Second argument: at least metaphysics seems nobler, since a science's nobility comes from its subject (De anima 1), and the subject of metaphysics is all being, whose goodness includes the goodness of any distinct being such as God.
claims: The whole of being seems a greater good than any distinct being, so metaphysics seems nobler than theology.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1552.summary: Third argument: the more proportioned an act is to its matter, the more it perfects it (De anima 2); other sciences, discoverable by natural reason, are more proportioned to us and so perfect the intellect more, making them worthier. Sed contra: all other sciences serve theology, so it is worthier.
claims: Sciences more proportioned to our natural reason seem to perfect us more.
That which all others serve is worthier than they.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1587.summary: Editorial 'Resolutio' summarizing the article: theology is worthier than other human sciences both by the dignity of its subject and by its mode of demonstration.
claims: Theology is worthier than other human sciences by dignity of subject and by mode of demonstration.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1598.summary: Opens the determinatio: a science's dignity derives either from its subject's nobility or from the certainty of its demonstration (De anima 1, with Averroes' example of geometry vs. astronomy); only the former concerns the present question, which is introduced on account of the subject. Theology clearly surpasses every special science in dignity of subject, since none has God as subject or directly considers him (sentence continues).
claims: A science's dignity comes either from its subject or from the certainty of its demonstrations.
No special science has God as subject, whereas theology does.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1657.summary: Completes the comparison with special sciences: since God surpasses all things in nobility, theology surpasses the special sciences in dignity.
claims: Theology exceeds the special sciences in dignity because God exceeds all in nobility.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1666.summary: Raises the harder case of metaphysics: since its subject, being qua being, includes both God and created good, it might seem worthier than theology, which is principally about God alone. To resolve this, Giles proposes two theses to be proved: that God and the whole universe are not a greater good than God alone, and that the theologian's knowledge of God is a greater good than all human sciences' knowledge of creatures together with their knowledge of God through creatures.
claims: God together with the universe is not a greater good than God alone.
The theologian's knowledge of God is a greater good than all human sciences' knowledge of creatures and of God through creatures.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1711.summary: First proof that God and the universe are not a greater good than God alone: all perfection derives from esse, and God as subsistent, unparticipated esse possesses every ratio of being and so every perfection (the 'universally perfect' of Metaph. 5, per Averroes); hence there is no more perfection, and no more goodness, in God plus creatures than in God alone — as Augustine says, God is the good of every good (De Trinitate 8).
claims: All perfections of all genera are gathered in the first principle.
God, as ipsum esse unparticipated, contains every ratio of perfection.
There is no more goodness in God and creatures together than in God alone.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1773.summary: Second proof, from the order of causes, begins: as power is appropriated to the efficient cause, goodness is appropriated to the end, since an end inclines by its perfection and goodness; whoever removes the end removes all good (Metaph. 2).
claims: Goodness is appropriated to the final cause as power is to the efficient cause.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1795.summary: Continues the second proof: Averroes identifies end and good; and just as among agent causes, when the lower agent has all its power from the higher, there is no greater power in both together than in the higher alone (sentence continues).
claims: End and good are the same.
When a lower agent has all its power from a higher, the two together have no more power than the higher alone.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1808.summary: Completes the second proof with the smith-and-hammer example: if the hammer had all its power from the smith, the smith could do without it whatever he could do with it; since God is the first efficient cause from whom all agents have their power, there is no more power in God and other agents than in God alone; and since God is likewise the last end from whom all beings have their goodness, there is no more goodness in God and the universe than in God alone.
claims: There is no more power in God and all other agents than in God alone.
As God is first efficient and last final cause, there is no more goodness in God and the universe than in God alone.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1854.summary: Third proof, from God's infinite goodness: divine goodness relates to created goodness not as line to line but as line to point, and just as line and point together are not greater than the line, created goodness adds nothing to the First's goodness — as Plato argued that pleasure is not the good since pleasure with prudence is greater (Ethics 10), a point Aristotle concedes of the separate good. Hence metaphysics, treating created and uncreated good together, is not worthier than theology; Giles announces two ways to show it is in fact baser: from theology's principal intention of God and from its mode of considering him.
claims: Divine goodness exceeds created goodness infinitely, as a line exceeds a point.
Created goodness adds nothing to the goodness of the First.
Metaphysics is not worthier than theology for including created good in its consideration.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e1937.summary: Shows theology is worthier than metaphysics in two ways and replies to the arguments. (1) From principal intention: what is per se and first is more (fire is hottest), so the theologian, considering God more primarily, knows as much and more of God than the metaphysician; knowledge of creatures adds nothing to knowledge of the First, and the surplus transcends all knowledge of creatures; like divine science itself, which would be debased by knowing anything outside itself primarily (Metaph. 12), theology is worthier for having God alone as principal object. (2) From mode of consideration: theology knows God by revelation, not reason, and so reaches truths inaccessible to metaphysics, more certain because seen in uncreated light. Replies: knowledge through causes is not greater than knowledge by revelation, since we can err about causes but divine revelation cannot deceive, and knowledge of principles exceeds knowledge of conclusions; God and the universe are not a greater good than God alone; metaphysics is more proportioned to our nature but not to nature elevated by grace, and the argument shows our weakness, not theology's indignity.
claims: The theologian knows as much of God as the metaphysician and more, and the surplus outweighs all knowledge of creatures.
Theology, like divine science, is worthier precisely because God alone is its principal object.
Revealed knowledge is more certain than rationally investigated knowledge, being seen in uncreated light.
Knowledge through causes is not superior to knowledge by revelation, since revelation cannot deceive.
Theology's lesser proportion to natural reason reflects our weakness, not its inferiority.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2154.summary: Rubric giving the title of Article 5: whether theology is one science.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2167.summary: First argument against theology's unity: it treats Creator and creature either under diverse rationes, making it several sciences, or under one ratio, in which case it could not know them distinctly and could not know God as distinct from creatures.
claims: Treating Creator and creature under one ratio would preclude distinguishing them; under diverse rationes would destroy theology's unity.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2204.summary: Second argument begins: according to Averroes on Metaph. 4, there is no single science of equivocals (sentence continues).
claims: There is no one science of equivocal things.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2212.summary: Completes the second argument: Averroes (De substantia orbis) holds that what is in celestial and terrestrial bodies is said equivocally; Creator and creature differ more than any bodies, or even than spirit and body (Hugh of St. Victor); so whatever is said of God and creature is wholly equivocal, and there is no one science of them.
claims: Since Creator and creature differ more than celestial and terrestrial bodies, predication of both is equivocal and precludes a single science.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2236.summary: Third argument: a science is one by being of one subject-genus (Post. An. 1), but corruptible and incorruptible differ more than in genus (Metaph. 10), and every creature compared to God is corruptible (Augustine); so there is no one science of created and uncreated.
claims: Created and uncreated differ more than generically, so cannot fall under one subject-genus.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2259.summary: Sed contra: what is not one science is not a science, since a thing has being and unity by the same (Metaph. 4); theology is a science; so it is one.
claims: Being a science and being one science are convertible.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2272.summary: Editorial 'Resolutio' summarizing the article: theology is one science by the unity of its object.
claims: Theology is one science by the unity of its object.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2279.summary: Opens the determinatio: theology must be granted to be one science, otherwise it would not be a science (the ratio of 'man' and 'one man' being the same, Sophistical Refutations); but assigning the mode of its unity is difficult and opinions vary.
claims: Theology must be one science, since a science that is not one is not a science.
The ground of theology's unity is disputed.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2308.summary: Reports the first opinion's framework: a threefold unity — of word only (equivocals), of word and thing but not ratio (analogicals, as 'being' names one thing, entity, found in all beings but under different rationes), and of word, thing, and ratio (univocals, as 'man'); equivocal unity precludes both a predicable and a subject-genus, analogical unity precludes a predicable genus (being is not a genus, Metaph. 3) but not a subject-genus (being is the subject of metaphysics), and univocal unity precludes neither.
claims: Equivocal unity is of word only; analogical of word and thing; univocal of word, thing, and ratio (per the reported opinion).
Analogical unity excludes a predicable genus but not a subject-genus.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2394.summary: States and refutes the first opinion's solution — that Creator and creature, though not univocally one, are analogically one and so can be the subject-genus of one science. It fails twice: the distinction is wrong, since analogical unity is not one nature found in all analogates (health is only in the animal, not the food) but unity of attribution to one thing (Metaph. 4); and it is irrelevant, since a science is one by analogy only if its subject is analogical, whereas God, theology's subject, is one thing and not an analogue.
claims: Analogical unity is unity of attribution to one thing, not a common nature present in all analogates.
Theology's subject, God, is not an analogical term, so analogy cannot ground its unity.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2453.summary: Second opinion: theology's unity is the unity of its light — as an inspired and revealed science, it is one because all such revelation originates from one divine light (sentence continues).
claims: (Reported opinion) Theology is one because all revelation derives from one divine light.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2473.summary: Refutes the unity-of-light opinion: a science has a twofold actuality, from its light and from its principal object; the light's actuality is general (one agent intellect actuates all human sciences), whereas specific unity comes from the subject, so sciences are divided as things are, not as lights; just as one agent-intellect light is compatible with specifically diverse human sciences, one divine light could be compatible with specifically diverse theologies — all the more since divine light exceeds our theology more than the agent intellect exceeds acquired science.
claims: A science's specific unity derives from its principal object, not from its light.
One light is compatible with many specifically distinct sciences.
The unity of the divine light therefore cannot ground theology's unity.
concepts: actuality from object vs. from light

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2551.summary: Refutes a revised version of the same opinion, that theology is one by the unity of a formal ratio of its object under which everything in it is comprehended: this begs the question, since the issue is precisely how all things can be united under one ratio in one science, so positing unity of ratio is equivalent to positing the unity of the science.
claims: Appealing to one formal ratio of the object to explain theology's unity begs the question.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2595.summary: Giles's own solution: human species, abstracted from sensibles, lead directly only to universal knowledge and do not give knowledge of what belongs to subordinate kinds as such, whereas separate substances can know through a universal species all that falls under it; hence for human sciences a common science does not render special sciences superfluous (metaphysics cannot tell us what belongs to mobile body as mobile), but if one science could know each thing under its proper ratio, there would be only one science in that genus. Theology, following the mode of divine wisdom with God as principal object, can consider each thing under its proper ratio, so in the genus of sciences resting on divine light there can be only one science, others being superfluous; theology is thus one by the unity of its object.
claims: Human species lead directly only to universal knowledge, unlike the species of separate substances.
Special human sciences are not superfluous because a common science cannot know things under their proper rationes.
Since theology can know all things under their proper rationes through God as principal object, only one science is possible in the genus resting on divine light.
Theology is one by the unity of its object.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2710.summary: Replies: (1) 'one ratio' may be formal or material; as sight sees white and black under the one formal ratio of color yet distinctly by diverse material rationes (and what is material for one power is formal for another, as taste and color for the common sense vs. the particular senses), so theology knows God and creatures under one formal ratio of the science but distinctly through diverse material rationes; (2) God and creatures are not truly equivocal but greatly analogous, or alternatively a science's unity comes from its principal object, which is God alone, not God and creature; (3) hence they need not be united in one genus, and Aristotle speaks there of predicable, not subject, genus. If parts and properties are required, metaphorically God functions as subject, the Trinity as parts, essential attributes as properties, and notional attributes as properties of the parts — though the likeness is slight and the unlikeness great.
claims: One science can know diverse objects distinctly under one formal ratio through diverse material rationes.
God and creatures are analogous, not purely equivocal.
Theology's unity derives from its principal object, God alone.
Metaphorically, the Trinity functions as theology's subject-parts, the essential attributes as properties, and notional attributes as properties of parts.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2866.summary: Rubric giving the title of Article 6: whether theology should be called a necessary science.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2873.summary: Arguments that no science beyond the philosophical disciplines is necessary: (1) sciences are divided as things, and the philosophical disciplines cover all things; (2) any further science would be common or special, but metaphysics already is the one common science and the special sciences sufficiently cover the parts of being.
claims: The philosophical disciplines already cover all things, both commonly and specially.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2912.summary: Sed contra: something is superfluous and vain if it does not attain its due end; theology most attains its due end; so it is most necessary.
claims: What attains its due end is not superfluous; theology most attains its end.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2925.summary: Editorial 'Resolutio' summarizing the article: theology can be called a necessary science.
claims: Theology can be called a necessary science.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e2933.summary: Distinguishes three senses of a necessary art: (1) one that supplies bodily need, opposed to arts for the sake of knowing — the mechanical arts (Metaph. 1); (2) one ordered to an extrinsic end, opposed to the 'honorable', so that among human sciences only metaphysics is honorable and the rest necessary ('the others are more necessary, none better'); (3) one that is not superfluous, because what it determines is not known in that way by another science.
claims: 'Necessary' can mean supplying bodily need, being ordered to an extrinsic end, or not being superfluous.
Among human sciences, metaphysics alone is honorable rather than necessary in the second sense.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e3011.summary: Answers by distinction: theology is not necessary in the first sense (only mechanical arts are) nor in the second (since all sciences serve it and it is ordered to none, it alone among wayfarers' sciences is honorable), but only in the third, as not superfluous; the senses are nested, so mechanical arts are necessary in three ways, invented speculative sciences in two, inspired theology in one. Giles reports three customary reasons for theology's non-superfluity — philosophers' science is mixed with error lacking the light of faith (Hugh); knowledge of God our end helps us reach it, as archers with a target (Ethics 1); faith and Scripture best proportion us to our end — but rejects them as per accidens, since they concern the science relative to us or its teachers, not the science in itself, just as the essential modes of philosophy are fixed though it could be taught otherwise.
claims: Theology is necessary only in the sense of not being superfluous; among wayfarers' sciences it alone is honorable.
The three senses of necessity are nested.
The customary reasons for theology's necessity (freedom from error, knowledge of our end, proportion to our end) are per accidens because they concern its relation to us.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e3180.summary: Gives the per se reason: a science is not superfluous if it gives knowledge of things not knowable by other sciences; theology gives knowledge of God to which the others cannot extend, so it is more necessary and less superfluous than they, in proportion as its knowledge of God surpasses theirs.
claims: A science is per se non-superfluous if it imparts knowledge unavailable from other sciences.
Theology is more necessary than other sciences because its knowledge of God exceeds theirs.

Gi9qrR-de3220-d1e3213.summary: Replies: (1) though human sciences treat all things, theology gives knowledge of things that they do not, so it is no more superfluous than particular sciences are given metaphysics; (2) the special sciences do not cover every part of being, since they do not consider God, and while metaphysics does, theology imparts knowledge of God that metaphysics cannot.
claims: Theology is not superfluous given human sciences, as special sciences are not superfluous given metaphysics.
Theology imparts knowledge of God that metaphysics cannot.

Gi9qrR-de3220-Dd1e175.summary: Article 1 establishes that theology is subalternated to no human science. Giles distinguishes three modes of subalternation — service to the science that considers the best in a genus (as all sciences serve metaphysics), the non-univocal quia/propter quid relation of Post. An. 1 (perspective under geometry, with its four conditions), and the quasi-univocal relation of subtle to coarse treatment (astronomy and sailors' star-lore) — and shows none applies: theology attains God more principally than metaphysics, its truths are above reason so no rational science gives their propter quid, it knows higher things of God, and no special science considers God at all. The replies explain theology's wonder by the height of its content and its borrowing from other sciences as ordering them to its service.
claims: There are three modes of subalternation: service, quia/propter quid, and subtle/coarse treatment of the same object.
Theology is subalternated to no human science in any mode.
Theology uses other sciences in its service rather than being regulated by them.

Gi9qrR-de3220-Dd1e840.summary: Article 2 argues that theology, as a science using the articles of faith as principles not evident to us, must be subalternated to a higher science in which they are evident — God's own knowledge or that of the blessed. This subalternation fits none of the human modes exactly (both sciences concern the best, and in God there is no quia/propter quid), but resembles all three analogically: the blessed grasp the same best object more fully, theology's principles are evident to them, and they see subtly what the theologian sees coarsely. The replies distinguish uncreated divine science from created science of wayfarers and the blessed, and theology's nobility in its genus from nobility simpliciter.
claims: Theology is subalternated to the science of God and of the blessed.
This subalternation resembles but does not coincide with any human mode.
Theology is noblest among wayfarers' sciences, not simpliciter.

Gi9qrR-de3220-Dd1e1138.summary: Article 3 concludes that the human sciences are subalternated to theology only in the first mode, by reason of the end. Analyzing why metaphysics subalternates the other sciences — it attains the best (God) and does so by reason's mode, thereby declaring their common principles — Giles shows theology shares the first ground but not the second, since it attains God by revelation; so all sciences, including metaphysics, serve theology and are taken into its service, metaphysics losing its status as the 'free' science, but theology does not declare their principles.
claims: Human sciences are subalternated to theology ratione finis, because it attains the highest good.
Theology does not supply the principles of the other sciences, since it attains God by revelation rather than by reason.
Compared to theology, metaphysics is a handmaid, not free.

Gi9qrR-de3220-Dd1e1475.summary: Article 4 establishes that theology is worthier than the other human sciences. It clearly surpasses the special sciences, none of which has God as subject; the harder case of metaphysics, whose subject being qua being includes created as well as divine good, is resolved by three proofs (from God's containing all perfection as unparticipated esse, from God as first efficient and last final cause, and from infinite divine goodness related to created goodness as line to point) that God plus the universe is not a greater good than God alone. Theology is then shown worthier both because it intends God principally (knowing as much and more of him than metaphysics, whose added knowledge of creatures adds nothing) and because it knows God by revelation in uncreated light, more certainly than by reason. The replies hold that revelation surpasses knowledge through causes and that theology's disproportion to natural reason shows our weakness, not its indignity.
claims: Theology is worthier than all human sciences, including metaphysics.
God and the universe together are not a greater good than God alone.
Theology is worthier both by its principal object and by its revealed mode of knowing.
Revealed knowledge is more certain than knowledge through causes.

Gi9qrR-de3220-Dd1e2146.summary: Article 5 holds, against arguments that theology's treatment of Creator and creature (equivocal, differing more than genus) destroys its unity, that theology is one science by the unity of its object. Giles rejects three rival accounts: unity of analogy (which misconstrues analogy as a common nature rather than attribution, and is irrelevant since God is not an analogous subject), unity of divine light (since one light is compatible with many specifically distinct sciences), and unity of formal ratio (which begs the question). His own account: unlike separate substances, humans cannot know specific features through universal species, so human sciences multiply; but theology, following divine wisdom with God as principal object, knows all things under their proper rationes, leaving room for only one science resting on divine light. The replies distinguish formal from material rationes, affirm analogy between God and creature, and metaphorically map subject, parts, and properties onto God, the Trinity, and the essential and notional attributes.
claims: Theology is one science by the unity of its object, God.
Analogy, unity of light, and unity of formal ratio cannot adequately explain theology's unity.
Because theology knows all things under their proper rationes, there can be only one science resting on divine light.
One science can know diverse objects distinctly under one formal ratio through diverse material rationes.

Gi9qrR-de3220-Dd1e2861.summary: Article 6 asks whether any science beyond the philosophical disciplines is necessary. Distinguishing three nested senses of 'necessary' — supplying bodily need, being ordered to an extrinsic end (opposed to 'honorable'), and not being superfluous — Giles concludes theology is necessary only in the third sense, being in the second sense the sole honorable science among wayfarers' sciences since all others serve it. He sets aside the customary reasons (philosophy's admixture of error, the value of knowing our end, our proportion to it) as per accidens, and grounds theology's non-superfluity per se in its imparting knowledge of God unavailable to any other science, including metaphysics.
claims: Theology is necessary only in the sense of being non-superfluous; it is the honorable science among wayfarers' sciences.
Theology's necessity rests per se on its imparting knowledge of God unavailable to other sciences.
Reasons for theology's necessity based on its relation to us are per accidens.

Gi9qrR-de3220.summary: Prologue, Question 2 examines what theology derives from its subject — order, dignity, unity, and necessity. On order (Arts. 1–3), Giles distinguishes three modes of subalternation and concludes that theology is subalternated to no human science, but is subalternated, in an analogical way resembling all three modes, to the science of God and the blessed, in which its principles (the articles of faith) are evident; conversely, all human sciences, including metaphysics, are subalternated to theology by reason of the end, serving it as handmaids, though it does not supply their principles because it knows God by revelation rather than reason. On dignity (Art. 4), theology surpasses all human sciences, including metaphysics, since God plus creation is no greater good than God alone and theology knows God both more principally and more certainly. On unity (Art. 5), theology is one by the unity of its object, God, through whom it knows all things under their proper rationes, rival accounts based on analogy, divine light, or formal ratio being rejected. On necessity (Art. 6), theology is necessary as non-superfluous, imparting knowledge of God unavailable elsewhere, and is the sole 'honorable' science of wayfarers.
claims: Theology is subalternated to no human science but to the science of God and the blessed.
All human sciences are subalternated to theology ratione finis as its handmaids.
Theology is worthier than every human science, including metaphysics.
Theology is one science by the unity of its object, God.
Theology is necessary as non-superfluous and is the honorable science among wayfarers' sciences.
